---
title: "Bootstrapping with Pokemon Cards"
format: html
---

![](pokemon.png){fig-align="center" width="750"}

## Description

Grab your students' attentions with a deck of Pokemon cards and start bootstrapping! Using physical, recognizable cards will allow students to identify what it means to sample with replacement. Plus, cards are easily shuffled and scrambled.

There are numeric values (HP - found in the top right corner) and categorical values (type, rarity, colour) that you can record data for on each card.

## Learning outcomes:

After the activity, students will be able to:

-   Identify that bootstrapping involves sampling with replacement

-   Calculate bootstrap sample means/proportions

## Materials Needed

-   Document Camera

-   50(ish) Pokemon (or other) cards.

-   Pen/paper or a white board

(Psst.. Are you at UBC? Ask Grace for a deck!)

## Directions

**Before class**

1.  Calculate a population quantity (mean or proportion) of all cards in your deck. Record this somewhere so you can reference it in class.

**In class**

2.  After introducing the bootstrapping algorithm in lecture, create a research question related to the Pokemon card (population) deck. **For example, what is the mean HP of my deck? Or, what proportion of my cards are electric type?**

3.  Take a small sample (10ish) from your deck (I ask 10 students to each pick one card). Put the rest aside and tell students that you won't touch any more cards for bootstrapping. Show the 10 cards under the document cam, emphasizing that each one is a unique Pokemon. Note the measurement of interest (HP, type)

4.  Calculate the sample mean/proportion of the 10 cards. Record it.

5.  Take the 10 cards and shuffle them. Draw one card, record the value of interest, and put the card back into the deck.

6.  Shuffle, choose, and record 9 more times. Note when the same card is chosen more than once!

7.  Take the 10 measurements and calculate the bootstrap mean/proportion. Record this on the paper/board as the first bootstrap mean/proportion.

8.  Repeat steps 5-7 once more, emphasizing that you did NOT take a new sample. Record this on the paper/board as the first bootstrap mean/proportion.

9.  Compare and contrast the two bootstrap estimates to each other.

    *They will likely differ.*

10. Compare the two bootstrap means/proportions to the **sample** mean/proportion.

    *With more samples, the bootstrap sample means/proportions would average out to this value.*

11. Compare the two bootstrap means/proportions to the **population** mean/proportion you calculated before class.

    *These may be quite different as the bootstrap means/proportions center around the sample mean, not the population one. If you get unlucky with your initial sample, then the bootstrap samples will be different from the population too.*
